messages.body_plain:
The issue here is that you have a massive factor variable along the x-axis. I noted recently that this causes major slow downs.
http://groups.google.com/group/ggplot2/browse_thread/thread/c35c47c7a3adf52f/d94d2a9c95176513?lnk=gst&q=mccreight+speed#d94d2a9c95176513

I'm assuming it's in the calculations, cause precomputing them you'll get a massive speed up.
http://groups.google.com/group/ggplot2/browse_thread/thread/3f002345b780db1f/f8282a77521e550f?lnk=gst&q=mccreight+boxplot#f8282a77521e550f

This later one is one i recommended for the examples on geom_boxplot, just to allude to the other thread i just posted on today.

I was recently in a similar position and found, only after the all the above, that line plots (different color lines at the hinges) contained as much information as boxplots. Looking at this many boxplots is a bit ridiculous, unless it's going to be put up on a wall i suppose.... just a side note.

James

messages.subject: Re: meaning of boxplot
messages.body_plain:
> I think it makes sense for this community to document ggplot and I would ask
> for some protocol for doing so as I can think of several things I'd
> immediately jump up and help document... actually, these are in other
> packages such as reshape as well, where I'm specifically thinking of the
> id.var argument which still remains obscure in documentation.
> It would also be tremendous if examples hashed out in the group could easily
> be added to the examples in the documentation, or there could be "further
> examples" or perhaps just links to threads on here.

If you're interested in helping document ggplot2, I'm slowly making it
easier and easier to get going.  I recently release the devtools
package to cran.  This means that you can easily install the version
of roxygen you need to produce the documentation:

install.packages("devtools")
library(devtools)
install_github("roxygen")

You then need to create a fork of the develop branch of ggplot2
(https://github.com/hadley/ggplot2/tree/develop), clone it on your
local computer, and you then you can modify the documentation.  In R

document("ggplot2")
dev_mode()
install("ggplot2")

will update the documentation, and reinstall so you can check your
changes.  You then commit you changes and issue a pull request.  This
takes a little bit of learning, but isn't too hard, and if you're
interested, I'm happy to get you up and running.

I have a student helping me out with documentation this summer.  You
can see what he's been working on at:
https://github.com/JakeRuss/ggplot2/commits/develop

> Ggplot has interesting documentation because what's in the pdf and in the
> help files (e.g. ?stat_boxplot) is a mere shadow of what's on the web page.

The web page is built from exactly the same sources that generate the
R documentation, so there shouldn't be any differences.  That said,
the website is a bit out of date, and that may account for a few
differences.

> Who uses the former?? I think it makes sense for the user community to have
> wiki version of the web documentation. Another possibility is having a repo
> on git hub for the html or having it in markdown. It would be a trememdous
> thing to be able to convert this into .Rd files. However, I'm not sure how
> that would interface with Roxygen documentation or if one would win out. I
> know almost nothing about Roxygen, other than these are ideas which might
> make it into Hadley's branch.

Github is making it easier and easier to make changes to source
online.  If you have a (free) github account, on any source file
you'll see a link to "edit this file", which allows you to edit on the
website, and then automatically send me a request to include your
change (https://github.com/blog/844-forking-with-the-edit-button).
Again, if anyone was interested in writing up instructions on how to
do this, I'd be happy to help out.

Hadley

--

Department of Statistics / Rice University

>
> ###############

> ggplot(dat) +
>  facet_wrap(~g) +
>  stat_contour(aes(x = x, y = y, z = z), breaks = 12)
> ###############
>
>
> In the meantime, Romain, if you just want nothing to be plotted in
> facets where the breaks are out of range, this seems to work for me at
> least in the few cases I tested.  Load ggplot2, then copy and paste
> the code below which will create a version of stat_contour in your
> workspace so it will be used over the one from ggplot2.  I added a
> small section that if all breaks are outside the range, it will issue
> a warning and return an empty data frame, which should have the side
> effect of nothing being plotted in that facet.  I attached the results
> I get from your example after using my modifaction.
>
> Hope this helps,
>
> Josh
>
>
> StatContour <- proto(Stat, {
>  calculate <- function(., data, scales, bins=NULL, binwidth=NULL,
> breaks = NULL, na.rm = FALSE, ...) {
>    data <- remove_missing(data, na.rm, name = "stat_contour")
>
>    # If no parameters set, use pretty bins
>    if (is.null(bins) && is.null(binwidth) && is.null(breaks)) {
>      breaks <- pretty(range(data$z), 10)
>    }
>    # If provided, use bins to calculate binwidth
>    if (!is.null(bins)) {
>      binwidth <- diff(range(data$z)) / bins
>    }
>    # If necessary, compute breaks from binwidth
>    if (is.null(breaks)) {
>      breaks <- fullseq(range(data$z), binwidth)
>    }
>    # section added to avoid errors when breaks are out of range
>    if (all(breaks < min(data$z) | breaks > max(data$z))) {
>      warning("All specified breaks are outside the range of z
>      no contours will be drawn in this plot/facet")
>      contour_df <- data.frame(level = NULL, x = NULL, y= NULL,
>        piece = NULL, group = NULL)
>      return(contour_df)
>    }
>
>    z <- tapply(data$z, data[c("x", "y")], identity)
>    cl <- contourLines(
>      x = sort(unique(data$x)), y = sort(unique(data$y)), z = z,
>      levels = breaks)
>    cl <- lapply(cl, as.data.frame)
>
>    contour_df <- rbind.fill(cl)
>    contour_df$piece <- rep(seq_along(cl), sapply(cl, nrow))
>    contour_df$group <- paste(data$group[1], contour_df$piece, sep = "-")
>    contour_df
>  }
>
>  objname <- "contour"
>  desc <- "Contours of 3d data"
>
>  icon <- function(.) GeomContour$icon()
>
>  default_geom <- function(.) GeomPath

>  required_aes <- c("x", "y", "z")
>  desc_outputs <- list(
>    level = "z value of contour"
>  )
> })

messages.body_plain:
On Wed, Jun 15, 2011 at 3:09 AM, Patrick Hausmann <c1...@uni-bremen.de> wrote:
> Dear list,
>
> I would like to make a dotchart and reorder the dots by difference
> between the two years "t2006" and "t2009". I found a solution, but
> it's a really hack. So I appreciate any hints
> for a better solution!!
>
> library(ggplot2)
> set.seed(123)
>
> x1 <- data.frame(id = LETTERS[1:14], time = "t2006",
> value=round(runif(14) * 100,0))
> x2 <- data.frame(id = LETTERS[1:14], time = "t2009",
> value=round(runif(14) * 100,0))
> x <- rbind(x1, x2)
>
> # Calculte the Difference between the two years (a really awful hack)
> x <- x[order(x$id, x$time),]
> ww <- x[x$time == "t2009", "value"] - x[x$time == "t2006", "value"]
> x$diff <- unlist(lapply(ww, FUN=function(x) df=c(NA, x)))
> x <- x[order(x$diff), ]
> xd <- x[!is.na <http://is.na>(x$diff), "id"]
> x$id <- factor(x$id, levels=xd)

One slightly more elegant approach is:

ddply(x, "id", summarise,
  diff = value[time == "t2006"] - value[time == "t2009"])

Hadley

> page - I don't think it belongs naturally in function-level
> documentation because it applies to multiple functions, and goes into
> more depth than you'd normally want in an example.

I agree, this is very nice!  I was just looking for the functionality
provided by label_parsed, as it happens :)

I do think some of this belongs in function-level documentation:
specifically, each of the stock label_* methods should have their own
?page, and the list you have under "Built-in acceptable values" should
appear, in its entirety, in ?facet_grid (and ?facet_wrap, if and when
it grows the same feature).

-- This is actually a general problem with the ggplot documentation,
both the ?pages and the website: reference documentation needs to
repeat itself a lot more than it currently does.  Every optional
argument to a function needs to have at least one sentence of
explanation in the documentation of that function, EVEN IF the primary
documentation of that argument is somewhere else.  Current bad
examples:

?geom_step:

# Arguments:
#      ...: other arguments

-- What other arguments?  Where do I look for documentation on what
the possibilities are and what happens to them?  Presumably all other
arguments are passed on to some other function (as is the common
pattern in R) but I have no idea which one.  (Some of the geoms'
documentation says "...: ignored", e.g. geom_linerange; that's more
helpful than just saying "other arguments" but leaves me wondering
*why* other arguments are ignored rather than rejected.)  It would
suffice, here, to write "...: all other arguments are passed on to
<name of function>".  Then I can go read that function's page for
details.

?facet_wrap:

# Arguments:
#   facets: NULL
# as.table: NULL
#    drop: NULL

This is obviously bad.  It's particularly bad here because 'facets' is
the primary knob for this function!  I can deduce its approximate
syntax from the examples (but not its *precise* syntax -- what happens
if I write "cyl ~" instead of "~ cyl", for instance? What happens if I
write "color ~ cut" instead of "~ color + cut"? and I can also deduce
what "drop" does, but I remain completely in the dark as to what
"as.table" does.)

I want to emphasize that this kind of thing is bad EVEN IF there is
some other documentation page where an explanation can be found,
because how do I know which page to look at?  Keep in mind that when
people are reading the reference manual instead of the ggplot2 book,
it's because they do more or less know how to use ggplot2 but they
cannot remember precisely how to do some specific thing; and do also
please keep in mind that not everyone has the book (or, in my case,
the book is currently on loan to someone else).

Having complained a whole lot, allow me also to say that if there's an
organized effort to improve the ggplot2 documentation, I would be
delighted to chip in.

zw

>> Josh

>>  calculate <- function(., data, scales, bins=NULL, binwidth=NULL,
>> breaks = NULL, na.rm = FALSE, ...) {

>>
>>    # If no parameters set, use pretty bins

>>      breaks <- pretty(range(data$z), 10)
>>    }
>>    # If provided, use bins to calculate binwidth
>>    if (!is.null(bins)) {
>>      binwidth <- diff(range(data$z)) / bins
>>    }
>>    # If necessary, compute breaks from binwidth
>>    if (is.null(breaks)) {
>>      breaks <- fullseq(range(data$z), binwidth)
>>    }
>>    # section added to avoid errors when breaks are out of range

>>      levels = breaks)
>>    cl <- lapply(cl, as.data.frame)
>>
>>    contour_df <- rbind.fill(cl)
>>    contour_df$piece <- rep(seq_along(cl), sapply(cl, nrow))
>>    contour_df$group <- paste(data$group[1], contour_df$piece, sep = "-")

>>  objname <- "contour"
>>  desc <- "Contours of 3d data"

messages.subject: Plotting ECDFs the same way plot(ecdf(...)) does it
messages.subject_clean: Plotting ECDFs the same way plot(ecdf(...)) does it
messages.body_plain:
Presently ggplot2 doesn't have any built-in logic for plotting
empirical CDFs.  The appropriate geom (geom_step) does exist, but
you've got to do the statistical reduction yourself, which is a little
fiddly.  More seriously, I can't find a good way to extend the
staircase to the left and right of the distribution, the way
plot.stepfun() does in base graphics.  For individual plots, I can
manually add points beyond the actual distribution as part of the
statistical reduction, and then use coord_cartesian to chop off the
graph at the left and right so it *looks* like the staircase goes all
the way to the edges; but this is awkward and doesn't work with
faceting.

(Attached are two screenshots of ECDFs from the same distribution -
one is what base graphics does, the other is the best approximation to
the same I've managed with ggplot2 and without manual coord_cartesian
limit adjustment; code to reproduce both is appended.  Note that I
don't insist on the dotted lines at y=0 and y=1.)

Can anyone suggest a better approach?

zw

ct <- c(2.32229, 5.01807, 5.32387, 5.69742, 6.39509, 6.9729,
    13.4403, 23.302, 23.3081, 34.9627, 37.3886, 41.102)
plot(ecdf(ct), verticals=TRUE, do.points=FALSE, main=NA)

ct2 <- structure(list(
    x = c(0, 2.32229, 5.01807, 5.32387, 5.69742, 6.39509,
    6.9729, 13.4403, 23.302, 23.3081, 34.9627, 37.3886, 41.102,
    44.2044), y = c(0, 0.0833333, 0.166667, 0.25, 0.333333, 0.416667,
    0.5, 0.583333, 0.666667, 0.75, 0.833333, 0.916667, 1, 1)),
    .Names = c("x", "y"), row.names=1:14, class = "data.frame")

ggplot(ct2, aes(x=x, y=y)) + geom_step() + ylab("Fn(x)")

Hi,
It seems like this should be easy, but it was actually a bit tricky
for me. Here is what I came up with:

co.occurance.count <- function(DF) {
  code <- as.character(DF$code)
  R <- as.data.frame(t(cbind(rbind(unique(code), unique(code)),
combn(code, 2))))
  names(R) <- c("code1", "code2")
  return(R)
}
tmp <- ddply(in.dat, .(ID), co.occurance.count)
out.dat <- as.data.frame(table(tmp[-1]))

Ugly but effective...

HTH,
Ista

messages.body_plain:
Hello Mahbubul,

It's not perfectly clear how you are counting your combinations from your example (check your A,B,C,D vectors in out.dat) but here is some code that shows a few different ways of doing the counts.  I think you want the 3rd option but am not totally sure from your example as you have a count of 4 for A vs A which is similar to options 2a, b and c.  This should be a fast and simple way of doing it.  The following code does the counts in 5 different ways, and Ista's makes a different and 6th way.

# CREATE TABLES OF COUNTS
A      <- table(in.dat)
Ared <- ifelse(A > 0, 1, 0)     # COUNTS GREATER THAN 1 ARE GIVEN THE VALUE OF 1 FOR THIS TABLE

# 1) MAXIMUM OF EACH (INCLUDES REPLACEMENT)
out.dat <- crossprod(A,A)

# 2a,b, c) COMBINATION COUNT OF EACH VALUE (ASYMMETRIC VERSION WHERE IF YOU HAVE TWO A's AND ONE B
#       IN AN ID FACTOR IT WOULD COUNT AS TWO FOR A VS B, BUT 1 FOR B VS A)
out.dat <- crossprod(A,Ared)  # OR
out.dat <- crossprod(Ared,A)  # OR MAX OF THE TWO WHICH WILL BE SYMMETRIC
out.dat <- ifelse(crossprod(A,Ared)>crossprod(Ared,A),crossprod(A,Ared),crossprod(Ared,A))

# 3) NUMBER OF UNIQUE COUNTS (ie IF YOU HAVE TWO A's AND ONE B IN AN ID FACTOR IT WOULD
#     COUNT AS ONE FOR A AND B)
out.dat <- crossprod(Ared,Ared)

# BASE VERSION PLOT
image(out.dat)

#GGPLOT2 VERSION
plot.dat <- melt(data.frame(cds = colnames(out.dat), values = out.dat))

qplot(cds,variable, geom="tile", fill=value,data=plot.dat, xlab="Codes", ylab="Codes")

There is likely a smoother way to plot matrices in ggplot than converting to a dataframe but I do not know it.

HTH,
Jonathan

> Hello Mahbubul,
> It's not perfectly clear how you are counting your combinations from your
> example (check your A,B,C,D vectors in out.dat) but here is some code that
> shows a few different ways of doing the counts.  I think you want the 3rd
> option but am not totally sure from your example as you have a count of 4
> for A vs A which is similar to options 2a, b and c.  This should be a fast
> and simple way of doing it.  The following code does the counts in 5
> different ways, and Ista's makes a different and 6th way.
> # CREATE TABLES OF COUNTS
> A      <- table(in.dat)
> Ared <- ifelse(A > 0, 1, 0)     # COUNTS GREATER THAN 1 ARE GIVEN THE VALUE
> OF 1 FOR THIS TABLE
> # 1) MAXIMUM OF EACH (INCLUDES REPLACEMENT)
> out.dat <- crossprod(A,A)
> # 2a,b, c) COMBINATION COUNT OF EACH VALUE (ASYMMETRIC VERSION WHERE IF YOU
> HAVE TWO A's AND ONE B
> #       IN AN ID FACTOR IT WOULD COUNT AS TWO FOR A VS B, BUT 1 FOR B VS A)
> out.dat <- crossprod(A,Ared)  # OR
> out.dat <- crossprod(Ared,A)  # OR MAX OF THE TWO WHICH WILL BE SYMMETRIC
> out.dat <-
> ifelse(crossprod(A,Ared)>crossprod(Ared,A),crossprod(A,Ared),crossprod(Ared,A))
> # 3) NUMBER OF UNIQUE COUNTS (ie IF YOU HAVE TWO A's AND ONE B IN AN ID
> FACTOR IT WOULD
> #     COUNT AS ONE FOR A AND B)
> out.dat <- crossprod(Ared,Ared)
> # BASE VERSION PLOT
> image(out.dat)
> #GGPLOT2 VERSION
> plot.dat <- melt(data.frame(cds = colnames(out.dat), values = out.dat))
> qplot(cds,variable, geom="tile", fill=value,data=plot.dat, xlab="Codes",
> ylab="Codes")

   from: https://github.com/hadley/ggplot2/wiki/Crime-in-Downtown-Houston,-Texas-:-Combining-ggplot2-and-Google-Maps

I'm on a Mac and I successfully managed to install rimage so that I
could run RgoogleMaps.

His code that sets up the Houston map is as follows:

CityHall_latlon <- c(lon = -95.369318, lat = 29.760210)
DowntownMap <-ggooglemap(center = CityHall_latlon, zoom = 14)

qplot(lon, lat, data = DowntownMap, geom = 'tile', fill = fill) +
  scale_fill_identity() +
  scale_x_continuous('Longitude') +
  scale_y_continuous('Latitude') +
  coord_equal() +
  opts(title = 'Terrain Map of Downtown Houston')

When I run this as is, I haven't had enough patience to wait for it to
complete.  I tried doing slices with subsets of DowntownMap[1:5000,].
I do get a ggplot with the correct thin slice of the google map in the
plot.  Based on some crude timing with different sizes, I estimate it
would take me over 7 hours to get the complete plot (running on my 2.8
GHz Intel Core 2 Duo iMac).  I've got 4 gig of RAM and while it runs
it looks like there is 1 gig of RAM free.

Does 7+ hours sound like a reasonable time estimate?

R version 2.13.0 (2011-04-13)
Platform: x86_64-apple-darwin9.8.0/x86_64 (64-bit)

[7] reshape_0.8.4       plyr_1.5.2

It has 640 x 640 tiles so maybe this speed is not unreasonable.  I
could run it over night.  One reason I am asking about this is that I
would swear that near the beginning of my experiments I got it to run
much more quickly on one occasion.  But after lots of additional
experimentation, I have concluded that's just another example of the
unreliability of eyewitness testimony.  Given that I had to fool

affected the speed.

messages.subject: scaling legend sample points
messages.body_plain:
Hello everybody,

Is it possible to change the size of the sample color splotches in the legend?

Here's a situation where you might want to do this (beware, this will
make a rather large pdf in your current working directory):

library(ggplot2)
quartz(height = 10, width = 20, file= "example.pdf", type = "pdf")
p <- ggplot(mtcars, aes(wt, mpg, colour = as.factor(cyl), size = 10))
p + geom_point() + scale_colour_hue("cylender")+ scale_size(legend = FALSE)
dev.off()

If you open the resulting pdf, you will see that the points on the
chart are size 10, but the points on the legend are still the default
size, (size = 2).

Is there any way to make the legend points the same size as the plot points?

Thank you,
Andrew

messages.subject: how to best present concentrated data points.
messages.subject_clean: how to best present concentrated data points.
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I am trying to plot a weighted density plot for two different types
and want to show the data points on the x axis.

The code is as follows. The data points will be very concentrated. Is
there a better way to present it( should I set the alpha value or
something else)?

Thanks

YL

library(ggplot2)
x <- rnorm(10000)
a <- rnorm(5000)
b <- rnorm(5000)
weights.x <- abs(a/sum(a))
weights.y <- abs(b/sum(b))
weight <- c(weights.x, weights.y)
ze <- rep(0,10000)
type <- c(rep("a",5000), rep("b",5000))
d <- data.frame(expo = x, weight = weight, type = type, ze = ze)
m <- ggplot(d, aes(x = expo, group = type, col = type, weight =
weight))
m+geom_density()+geom_point(aes(x = expo, y = ze, shape = type))

messages.subject: Legend display with two dataframes
messages.body_plain:
Hello there,

I have a plot like the one below where I have raw data points displayed as small grey points and some summary statistics displayed as larger black points. These figures display beautifully using ggplot2. The only issue is in the legend. Running the example below illustrates that one of the points (unfilled diamond) doesn't look quite right in the legend. The smaller grey point is being displayed inside the larger point. I imagine that this is happening also in the filled points, but that the grey point is just not visible.

Can anyone recommend a way to remove the grey points from the legend while retaining the black filled points?

Thanks in advance.

Sam

#Some data
dat <- data.frame(x = runif(270, 0, 125), z = rep(LETTERS[1:3], each = 3),
 yy = letters[1:3], stringsAsFactors = TRUE)

#mean and statistic
summ <- ddply(dat, .(z, yy), summarise, m = mean(x), sd = sd(x))
#plot
ggplot(data = summ, aes(x = yy, y = x)) +
    geom_point(data=summ, aes(group=z,shape = z), size = 3, position = position_dodge(width = 0.8)) +
    geom_errorbar(data=summ,aes(ymin = m - sd, ymax = m + sd), width = 0.5, size = 0.5,  position = position_dodge(width = 0.8)) +
    geom_point(data=dat, aes(x= yy, y=x, shape=z, group=z), alpha=0.4,position = position_dodge(width = 0.8)) +
    scale_shape_manual(value=c(19,5,17))

messages.body_plain:
-----BEGIN PGP SIGNED MESSAGE-----
Hash: SHA1

  Just wondering if there was any update on the possibility of plotting
log-scaled axes without scientific notations, and with breaks that are
pretty on the original scale, as in these threads:

http://groups.google.com/group/ggplot2/browse_thread/thread/658aac9db56065b/fcf69c35ae0898e4?lnk=gst&q=scale_y_log10+breaks+pretty#fcf69c35ae0898e4

http://groups.google.com/group/ggplot2/browse_thread/thread/f0a5d89133c600ed/3a820d0ab05e5d8d?lnk=gst&q=scale_y_log10+formatter#3a820d0ab05e5d8d

  This is my current solution, which could probably be tweaked a bit:
the guts are mostly drawn from the example in ?axTicks which replicates
the internal calculations that base R does for pretty log axis ticks ...

lsc <- function(limit,...) {
  get_axp <- function(x) 10^c(ceiling(x[1]), floor(x[2]))
   ## mimic par("yaxs")=="i"
   usr.i <- log10(limit)
   (aT.i <- axTicks(side=2, usr=usr.i,
                    axp=c(get_axp(usr.i), n=3), log=TRUE))
   scale_y_log10(breaks=aT.i,labels=format(aT.i,scientific=FALSE,
trim=TRUE, drop0trailing=TRUE))
}

 ??
  Ben Bolker

Yes, this will be the default in the next version of ggplot2.

If you want to try out the latest version, it's not too difficult to do:

install.packages("devtools")
library(devtools)

install_github("devtools") # get latest dev version of devtools
# may need to restart R here (not sure)
install_github("scales") # get new scales package

dev_mode() # switch to dev mode so you don't kill your existing install
install_github("ggplot2", branch = "develop")

library(ggplot2)
qplot(mpg, wt, data = mtcars) + scale_x_log10()

(you'll need R 2.13, and if on windows, you'll need to have installed Rtools)

If it doesn't work, please let me know so I can fix the instructions -
I would like to make it easier for people to try out the development
version.

Hadley

messages.subject: Re: boxplot: how to get vertical lines at the end of the whiskers?
messages.subject_clean: boxplot: how to get vertical lines at the end of the whiskers?
messages.body_plain:
Hi:

(a) The definition of the boxplot in geom_boxplot() is the same as
that in graphics::boxplot().
(b) If you save a boxplot() to an object, it will return a list whose
first component is a matrix that includes the positions of the
whiskers.

That information can be transferred to a data frame which can be used
as input to geom_segment() to produce whiskers for the boxplots.
Here's a reproducible example using the built-in InsectSprays data:

bpstat <- boxplot(count ~ spray, data = InsectSprays)
str(bpstat)   # the stats component contains the positional info
bpstat$stats
whiskers <- with(bpstat, data.frame(spray = names,
                                    lower = stats[1, ],
                                    upper = stats[5, ]))

ggplot(InsectSprays) + geom_boxplot(aes(x = spray, y = count)) +
   geom_segment(data = whiskers, aes(x = as.numeric(spray) - 0.1,
                                     y = lower,
                                     xend = as.numeric(spray) + 0.1,
                                     yend = lower)) +
   geom_segment(data = whiskers, aes(x = as.numeric(spray) - 0.1,
                                     y = upper,
                                     xend = as.numeric(spray) + 0.1,
                                     yend = upper))

Longer whiskers are obtained by increasing the value from 0.1 to
whatever suits you.

HTH,
Dennis

messages.subject: Histogram axis problems...
messages.body_plain:
Hey everyone

With a little help from the group, I have produced a single column of
faceted histograms with ggplot2. Please see my script below. I have
removed all gridlines and background. However, I have some axis
formatting issues:

1) is it possible to change the frequency of major tick mark labels?
For example, "xlim(0, 460)" puts tick marks and labels every 100, I
would prefer every 25.
2) is it possible to insert minor tick marks (without labels) at the
same location as my binwidth, i.e. every 5?
3) the x axis is only plotted on the bottom facet. Is it possible to
plot the x axis and its tick marks on each facet?
4) there is a gap between the plotted data and the x and y axis. Is it
possible to remove this gap? For example, if using axis function in R:
base graphics, this would be achieved using "pos = 0"

Any help would be gratefully received!!!

Kind regards,

Jonathan

plotfunc <- function(site) {
    ggplot(DATA[DATA$Site == site, ], aes(x = Length)) + xlim(0, 460)
+
    geom_histogram(binwidth = 5) +
    facet_grid(Survey.year ~ .) +
    labs(x = "Length class (5-mm groups)", y = "Frequency") +
    opts(axis.text.x = theme_text(angle = 90, family = "serif"),
axis.text.y = theme_text(family = "serif"), axis.title.x =
theme_text(family = "serif"), axis.title.y = theme_text(angle = 90,
family = "serif"), axis.line = theme_segment(), axis.ticks =
theme_segment(), panel.background = theme_blank(), panel.grid.minor =
theme_blank(), strip.text.y = theme_text(family = "serif"),
strip.background = theme_blank(), axis.text.y = theme_text(),
axis.text.x = theme_text())
  ggsave(paste(site, ".wmf", sep=""), path = "C:/R", width = 6.2,
height = 8.7)
}

sitelist <- as.list(unique(DATA$Site))
l_ply(sitelist, .fun = plotfunc)

messages.subject: Re: problem with facet_wrap
messages.body_plain:
On 6/30/2011 1:16 PM, James Rome wrote:
> Dear list,
>
> I have the following code:
>
> ncolsm = 3
> title="MyTitle"
> colours<- c(AS = "red", RF = "brown", AF =383, PH="cyan",PF = "black",
>     BA = "green", FI = "blue", FF = 56, PS = "magenta", TC=94)
> shapes<- c(AS = "A", RF = "R", AF = "f", PH="H", PF = "P",
>      BA = "B", FI = "I", FF = "F", PS = "S", TC="T")
> pp = qplot(as.numeric(PredTime), as.numeric(dt), data=dss, color=MsgType,
>               main=title, ylab="Error (min)", shape=MsgType,
> alpha=I(1/2), xlim=c(0,60),
>              xlab="Time before ON (min)", ylim=c(-40, 40))  +
>              scale_size(to=c(2., 2.), legend=FALSE) +
>              scale_colour_manual(value = colours) +
> scale_shape_manual(value=shapes)
>
> pp2 = pp + facet_wrap(~ msgType, ncol=ncolsm)
>
> pp plots properly.
> But pp2 gives:
>> pp2
> Error in `[.data.frame`(plot$data, , setdiff(cond, names(df)), drop =
> FALSE) :
>    undefined columns selected
>> unique(dss$MsgType)
>   [1] AS PF RF AF BA FI FF TC PS PH
> Levels: PH<  PS<  AS<  BA<  PF<  RF<  AF<  FI<  FF<  TC
>
> How does one go about debugging such an error?

The error hints that a column in the data was requested that doesn't
exist. (OK, hint may be too strong.  That construct is from using
subsetting on a dataframe with column names, and the error is what you
get if you specify a column name that doesn't exist.)

So looking at your code to make sure all the columns (variables) you
request are there, and knowing that the difference is between pp and
pp2, I notice that the only additional variable (from the data) in pp2
is msgType.  I also notice that in the previous plot, there is variable
MsgType (note initial capital).  Checking the data you attached, there
is only a MsgType, no msgType.  So it should be:

pp2 <- pp + facet_wrap(~ MsgType, ncol=ncolsm)

Yes, a long way to say you made a typo.  But you asked how to go about
debugging such an error.

> Thanks,
> Jim Rome
>

--
Brian S. Diggs, PhD
Senior Research Associate, Department of Surgery
Oregon Health & Science University

> removed all gridlines and background. However, I have some axis
> formatting issues:
>
> 1) is it possible to change the frequency of major tick mark labels?
> For example, "xlim(0, 460)" puts tick marks and labels every 100, I
> would prefer every 25.

Yes, change xlim() to scale_x_continuous(limits = c(0, 460), breaks = seq(0, 460, by =25))

> 2) is it possible to insert minor tick marks (without labels) at the
> same location as my binwidth, i.e. every 5?

add minor_breaks =  seq(0, 460, by 5) inside of scale_x_continuous

> 3) the x axis is only plotted on the bottom facet. Is it possible to
> plot the x axis and its tick marks on each facet?

No, is not possible

> 4) there is a gap between the plotted data and the x and y axis. Is it
> possible to remove this gap? For example, if using axis function in R:
> base graphics, this would be achieved using "pos = 0"

put expand = c(0,0) inside scale_y_continuous and scale_y_continuous.
